evaluations.query: Why is material science such a critical problem for Neuralink?
evaluations.golden_response: I think it's going to be important in terms of material science problems, is making sure that the threads so the electrodes, can last for decades in the brain, which is a tricky thing because it's a very corrosive environment and you're in a dichotomy where you want to read, and you want to send electrical signals, and you want to generate electrical signals. But you don't want to corrode the electrodes over time. So, you need to have an insulating layer that is very robust but also very, very thin. It has to be just the right amount of insulation, and it has to stay that amount of insulation over time. So that's why we think probably like a silicon carbide type insulator is probably the best long term from a material science standpoint. But silicon carbide is tough material to work with. But that's probably the right choice long-term.

fast.response: We need to be able to survive inside the skull. The skull is very hard, so we have to make something that can drill through it. So, we've been working on this for quite some time, and I think we have made significant progress. We're really pushing the limits of what we thought was possible.

thinking.response: Well, it's not exactly material science, but we need to understand the biocompatibility of things. So, what is this thing going into your skull? It needs to not harm your brain. And I think people have underestimated the importance of biocompatibility. Like, why did they put lead into gasoline? Because it was cheap. Why did they put asbestos in insulation? Because it was cheap. So, there's no reason why we shouldn't do better than that. We should try to get the best materials possible. Now, we're trying to put something that's essentially a tiny robot into your skull. That's a pretty big deal. So, we want to make sure it's safe and doesn't damage your brain.

fast.response: Well, I think we're talking about the Boring Company's high-speed tunneling project here. The electrode spacing is around 10 mm.

thinking.response: The electrode threads for the Neuralink brain-machine interface are quite thin. I think they're around 50 microns or something like that. So, it's not like a big needle. thinking.response: Well, I think it's extremely important to have the ability to upgrade the Neuralink chip because we're just starting to get into this new paradigm where we're going to have machines talking to each other all the time, not just humans talking to machines, but also machines talking to each other. Now, we're going to have devices in the body that can communicate with each other directly. So, you want to be able to upgrade your own devices in your body. It makes sense. evaluations.query: What are the read and write speeds of the Neuralink device?
evaluations.golden_response: Well, do you want to say things like time resolution, like, you know, within how many milliseconds can you detect a spike. In terms of the signals that we're collecting, we're digitizing them at 20 kilohertz. The signals of interest are anywhere between about a millisecond in width. We sort of sample it at 20 times that speed. And we have analog to digital converters that divide that into 1024 levels, so 10-bit resolution. And the spike detection is done in less than 900 nanoseconds, which is really, really fast.

fast.response: Well, I think the maximum write speed is around 100 megabytes per second, but that's only for reading from storage. If we can actually interface directly with the brain, it's possible that the write speed will be much higher than that. And it may even exceed what the human brain can handle. But currently, I think the maximum write speed of the implant is about 100 megabytes per second.

thinking.response: Well, I think we've been pretty clear on this. We can read at rates of up to 100 megabytes per second. And we can write at rates of 1 gigabyte per second. So, it's very fast, but it's also quite intuitive. And then, of course, the neural interface will allow us to read thoughts from your brain directly. evaluations.query: How does larger vocabulary increase effective bit rate?
evaluations.golden_response: Well, it depends on the person. You can speak very fast. Like we can communicate very quickly. And also, if you use a wide range of vocabulary, your effective bit rate is higher. If there's a single word that is able to convey something that would normally require, I don't know, 10 simple words, then you've got maybe a 10X compression on your hands. And that's really like with memes. Memes are like data compression.

fast.response: The bit rate of text is basically how many bits per character. So, if you've got a very long vocabulary, you can encode each character in fewer bits. For example, if you go back to ASCII characters, you know, we had eight bits per character, where each letter was represented by three bytes. Now we have sixty-four bits per character, which makes a huge difference. I think it's five times faster, actually. And that's why our text-to-speech model is significantly faster and better quality than anything that existed before. And then with Grok, we've also gotten to sixty-four bits per character, which makes a huge difference in the density of the model.

thinking.response: The key is you want to use more bits per second for each byte of data because if you have more words per sentence, then there's less whitespace which means you can encode the data more efficiently. The answer is it depends on the situation but generally speaking, having more words per sentence increases the effective bit rate. It really depends on how well the text is written. If the writing is not good, that won't make a difference. But in general, having more words per sentence increases the effective bit rate.
